parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Cranberries

The story of a unique North American crop

Cranberries are among the few fruits native to North America to have been cultivated commercially for centuries. These small, crimson berries flourish only under a narrow set of environmental conditions, particularly in sandy, acidic soil. This type of ground drains readily while retaining enough moisture for the plants' shallow roots. Because ordinary farmland rarely provides this balance, cranberries are generally grown in low-lying areas known as bogs. These natural basins, bordered by gentle ridges, enable growers to control water levels precisely. The resulting environment is quite different from that required by most other fruit crops.

Many bogs used for cranberry farming were created thousands of years ago when retreating glaciers carved deep hollows known as kettle ponds. Over time, layers of sand and clay formed within these basins, creating a natural filtration system that helps keep pollutants out of the water. The clay floor serves as a barrier, preventing harmful substances from entering the pond and helping to preserve the clean water needed by healthy vines. Together with deliberate control of water levels, these geological features make kettle-pond sites particularly suitable for cranberry cultivation.

Long before European settlement, Wampanoag communities used cranberries in several practical ways. The fruit could be dried and combined with other foods, allowing it to be kept for periods when fresh plants were scarce. These methods produced compact foodstuffs that could be consumed during colder months. Cranberries also played a role in first aid: crushed fruit was applied to sores and minor wounds, reflecting practical knowledge of its cleansing qualities.

When European settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, they found cranberries growing in coastal hollows and quickly recognised their usefulness. Rather than trying to establish European varieties, they adopted the native species already suited to local conditions. Colonists used the fruit in preserves and beverages and valued its nutritional contribution during winter voyages and periods of food shortage inland. Over time, cranberries became part of colonial cooking and later of North American holiday traditions.

In the early nineteenth century, planned cultivation expanded through local experimentation. Captain Henry Hall, a Massachusetts grower, noticed that windblown sand falling onto his cranberry beds improved both fruit quality and yield. He began spreading sand deliberately and found that it improved soil texture while reducing pest problems. Hall's manipulation of the land and surface materials represented an important step towards systematic cranberry farming.

Cranberry production follows a seasonal routine in which each operation is closely linked to weather conditions. In winter, farmers often flood the bogs. As the water freezes, it forms an insulating layer that protects the vines from severe cold and drying winds. Sand may also be spread across the frozen surface so that, after thawing, it works down into the bed, improving drainage and helping new shoots become established. Growers also clear trees and scrub from around the bogs, allowing air to circulate more freely and reducing humidity, which helps lower the risk of disease.

In spring, the frozen cover is managed and water levels are adjusted. Growers may apply water during vulnerable periods to protect emerging shoots from sudden frosts. They also carry out routine maintenance on channels, pumps and irrigation lines and take measures to limit pest pressure before the plants enter full growth. By early summer, the vines are active and attention shifts to the even development of the fruit. Farmers inspect the beds for weeds that would compete with the crop and remove them promptly to protect potential yields.

As autumn approaches, ripening fruit signals the start of harvest. In many operations, the bogs are flooded again so that the buoyant berries rise to the surface and can be separated from the vines more easily. Although mechanical aids and modern equipment have altered some aspects of the work, successful cranberry production continues to depend on a careful balance between soil conditions, water management and human intervention. From the practical uses developed by the Wampanoag to the innovations of later growers, cranberry cultivation remains closely tied to seasonal management of a distinctive landscape.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Australia's camouflaged creatures

Many species of animals in Australia protect themselves by using camouflage—a way of ‘hiding’ by blending into their surroundings.

A

Most species use camouflage to some extent. If they are convincing, they survive to pass their genes on to future generations. After generations of natural selection, animals can develop astonishingly complex camouflage techniques, manipulating shape, colour and movement. ‘The principle of camouflage is to make it economically unviable for a predator to pursue a particular species of prey,’ explains Professor Mark Elgar of the University of Melbourne. ‘Camouflage increases the search time and, as a consequence, the predator will simply target another species, either because it does not see the camouflaged individual or because it finds something more obvious to pursue.’

B

The easiest way for an animal to disguise itself is to become effectively invisible in its surroundings. To that end, stick and leaf insects have evolved complex camouflage to hide themselves from predators. Many have the texture of sticks or dry leaves, while others imitate living foliage, even the veins in a leaf. Some insects develop blemishes to match the spots caused by disease. A convincing appearance works only if its owner also acts the part, so during the day a creature using this type of camouflage remains motionless or sways like a dead leaf in the breeze. If disturbed, it falls to the ground and stays still. Entomologist Paul Zborowski, who has spent decades photographing inconspicuous creatures, rates the desert insects of Central Australia as the most convincingly disguised creatures he has seen. ‘It is an incredibly old habitat, so the creatures have had a long time to adapt,’ Zborowski explains. Most of them behave like stones and remain motionless throughout the day, feeding only at night.

C

A tawny frogmouth sitting motionless on a stump also illustrates the importance of pairing a convincing appearance with appropriate behaviour. Professor Gisela Kaplan of the University of New England in Australia says the frogmouth's skill at camouflage involves learned behaviour. Although adopting a pose may be a reflex and can be observed during a hatchling's first week, the ability to choose a background that matches its colouration does not develop for four to six months. When the chicks land, they are usually highly conspicuous, and their parents try to signal to them to move to a safer location.

D

Fixed camouflage is effective only in a relatively unchanging environment, so some animals, such as the cuttlefish, have evolved an adaptable disguise. The cuttlefish can almost instantly change its colour, pattern and texture to match its surroundings, using specialised cells and muscles. On Queensland's reefs, scientists have been studying another ocean dweller that changes colour, although not in order to blend into its surroundings. Dr Karen Cheney of the University of Queensland says the bluestriped fangblenny alters its colouration to mimic other species of fish, allowing it to travel with them and benefit from safety in numbers. Its most impressive impersonation is of the black-and-neon-blue-striped cleaner wrasse, which eats parasites found on larger fish. Not only does the fangblenny benefit from the reduced predation associated with the wrasse's beneficial relationships with other fish, but the disguise also allows it to get closer to its prey. It darts out from the safety of the wrasse's cleaning station to nip at unsuspecting fish passing by, but does not attack those coming to be cleaned.

E

The most famous form of mimicry, however, is used for defence rather than attack. Batesian mimicry refers to animals that gain protection from predators by imitating a dangerous organism, often using conspicuous colours. The nineteenth-century naturalist Henry Bates first suggested this camouflage technique after noticing that several Amazonian butterfly species looked alike. The technique was later named after him. In Australian waters, the harmless harlequin snake eel has the same black-and-white bands as the highly toxic yellow-lipped sea krait, helping to deter predators. However, the success of Batesian mimicry depends on the ratio of mimics to originals. If a predator encounters too many mimics that are edible, it may simply assume that none of the animals with those markings are dangerous, explains Martyn Robinson, an educational naturalist with the Australian Museum.

F

An imitation of a more dangerous creature need not be exact; it only has to be convincing enough to make a potential predator hesitate. The hawk moth caterpillar has markings resembling a snake's eyes on its abdomen. When confronted, the caterpillar pulls its head in and the ‘eyes’ flash open. Whether the potential predator thinks it has seen a snake or is simply startled is unclear, but the outcome is that the caterpillar lives to see another day.

G

In Queensland's Tablelands, the chameleon gecko has another way of making predators hesitate. Its body is brown, but its tail is banded in black and white. Robinson explains that, if attacked, the chameleon gecko drops its tail, which then wriggles around on the ground. Many lizards do this, but in the case of the chameleon gecko, the tail bones actually rub against one another, causing it to squeak. ‘The predator is, of course, thoroughly absorbed by this black-and-white-striped, wriggling, squeaking thing on the ground, and the gecko can sneak away,’ Robinson says. It is a one-time-only trick: the regrown tail is brown, the same colour as the gecko's body. Such precise disguise and elaborate trickery illustrate the limitless possibilities of nature. But, as Robinson points out, only the most successful illusionists are here to tell the tale.

A convincing appearance works only if its owner also acts the part, so during the day a creature using this type of camouflage remains motionless or sways like a dead leaf in the breeze. If disturbed, it falls to the ground and stays still. Entomologist Paul Zborowski, who has spent decades photographing inconspicuous creatures, rates the desert insects of Central Australia as the most convincingly disguised creatures he has seen. ‘It is an incredibly old habitat, so the creatures have had a long time to adapt,’ Zborowski explains. Most of them behave like stones and remain motionless throughout the day, feeding only at night.

C

A tawny frogmouth sitting motionless on a stump also illustrates the importance of pairing a convincing appearance with appropriate behaviour. Professor Gisela Kaplan of the University of New England in Australia says the frogmouth's skill at camouflage involves learned behaviour. Although adopting a pose may be a reflex and can be observed during a hatchling's first week, the ability to choose a background that matches its colouration does not develop for four to six months. When the chicks land, they are usually highly conspicuous, and their parents try to signal to them to move to a safer location.

D

Fixed camouflage is effective only in a relatively unchanging environment, so some animals, such as the cuttlefish, have evolved an adaptable disguise. The cuttlefish can almost instantly change its colour, pattern and texture to match its surroundings, using specialised cells and muscles. On Queensland's reefs, scientists have been studying another ocean dweller that changes colour, although not in order to blend into its surroundings. Dr Karen Cheney of the University of Queensland says the bluestriped fangblenny alters its colouration to mimic other species of fish, allowing it to travel with them and benefit from safety in numbers. Its most impressive impersonation is of the black-and-neon-blue-striped cleaner wrasse, which eats parasites found on larger fish. Not only does the fangblenny benefit from the reduced predation associated with the wrasse's beneficial relationships with other fish, but the disguise also allows it to get closer to its prey. It darts out from the safety of the wrasse's cleaning station to nip at unsuspecting fish passing by, but does not attack those coming to be cleaned.

E

The most famous form of mimicry, however, is used for defence rather than attack. Batesian mimicry refers to animals that gain protection from predators by imitating a dangerous organism, often using conspicuous colours. The nineteenth-century naturalist Henry Bates first suggested this camouflage technique after noticing that several Amazonian butterfly species looked alike. The technique was later named after him. In Australian waters, the harmless harlequin snake eel has the same black-and-white bands as the highly toxic yellow-lipped sea krait, helping to deter predators. However, the success of Batesian mimicry depends on the ratio of mimics to originals. If a predator encounters too many mimics that are edible, it may simply assume that none of the animals with those markings are dangerous, explains Martyn Robinson, an educational naturalist with the Australian Museum.

F

An imitation of a more dangerous creature need not be exact; it only has to be convincing enough to make a potential predator hesitate. The hawk moth caterpillar has markings resembling a snake's eyes on its abdomen. When confronted, the caterpillar pulls its head in and the ‘eyes’ flash open. Whether the potential predator thinks it has seen a snake or is simply startled is unclear, but the outcome is that the caterpillar lives to see another day.

G

In Queensland's Tablelands, the chameleon gecko has another way of making predators hesitate. Its body is brown, but its tail is banded in black and white. Robinson explains that, if attacked, the chameleon gecko drops its tail, which then wriggles around on the ground. It is a one-time-only trick: the regrown tail is brown, the same colour as the gecko's body. Such precise disguise and elaborate trickery illustrate the limitless possibilities of nature. But, as Robinson points out, only the most successful illusionists are here to tell the tale.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

The Effectiveness of Online Courses

As access to the internet expanded, web-based learning grew rapidly. One set of estimates suggested that approximately half of households in the United States—representing around 150 million people—had internet access, while about two million students were taking post-secondary courses delivered entirely online. Millions more at primary, secondary and post-secondary levels were participating in some form of online education. Despite this growth, questions remain about the effectiveness of online courses, particularly in relation to individual students' needs, perceptions and learning outcomes.

Two central features of learning in a conventional classroom are the social and communicative interactions between students and teachers and among students themselves. Asking a question, sharing an opinion with a fellow student, or disagreeing with a point of view in a reading assignment are all fundamental learning activities. In web-based education, however, both students and teachers may need to adapt their behaviour if such interactions are to occur successfully. Many online courses therefore provide electronic bulletin boards or discussion forums through which students can communicate with instructors and with one another.

Although most studies have found a relationship between interaction and satisfaction in web-based courses, some researchers caution that interaction is not automatically beneficial. Ruberg, Taylor and Moore, for example, argue that students must adjust to the nonlinear nature of online learning. Unlike a conventional discussion that may concentrate on a single topic at a time, an online session can contain several discussion threads developing simultaneously. Students may respond not only to the teacher but also to different classmates, depending on their interests and points of view.

Sproull and Kiesler warn that inaccurate information may continue to circulate in online discussions because an instructor cannot always correct or clarify a comment immediately. Students therefore need sufficient experience and knowledge to distinguish reliable contributions from misinformation. The sheer volume of interaction can create a further difficulty: information overload. Online comments also tend to be longer than those made in face-to-face discussions. Faced with large quantities of material from many different sources, students must pay close attention both to who is contributing and to what is being said. As the economist Herbert Simon observed, “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.”

Research into interaction has also focused on the concept of presence—the sense of being in a particular place and of belonging to a group. It is often assumed that students attending a face-to-face course experience a stronger sense of belonging than those studying online. A student who is physically present can listen to others, raise a hand to comment or ask a question, and develop relationships during breaks and other informal moments. Physical attendance, however, does not guarantee such a feeling: some students may still experience alienation in a conventional classroom.

The concept of presence has therefore been redefined in relation to online learning. In its simplest form, it refers to a student's sense of being enrolled in and belonging to a course, together with the ability to interact with others despite the absence of physical contact. The concept has since broadened to include forms such as telepresence, cognitive presence, social presence and teaching presence. Closely related is the idea of community, which refers to groups such as the students taking a particular course. In online education, this has led to terms such as communities of inquiry, communities of learners and knowledge-building communities.

As definitions of presence have expanded, researchers have increasingly distinguished presence from interaction. The two concepts are related, but they are not identical. Interaction may provide evidence of presence, yet a student can participate actively in online exchanges without necessarily feeling that he or she belongs to the class or group.

Professor Anthony Picciano investigated these issues using questionnaires to examine students' attitudes towards interaction and learning in online courses. His study went beyond participants' perceptions by also measuring social presence, participation in course activities and actual academic performance. Although previous research generally supports a strong relationship between perceived interaction and perceived learning, Picciano's results showed that the relationship between actual interaction and performance is mixed.

Interaction remains an important component of many online courses. Nevertheless, exactly how it affects learning outcomes—and how closely the two are related—remains uncertain and requires further investigation.
